claim: The encapsidation of HIV-1 gRNA into virions is enabled by the binding of the nucleocapsid (NC) domain of the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein to the structured viral RNA packaging signal (Ψ) at the 5' end of the viral genome.
source: The encapsidation of HIV-1 gRNA into virions is enabled by the binding of the nucleocapsid (NC) domain of the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein to the structured viral RNA packaging signal (Ψ) at the 5' end of the viral genome.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: NC alone does not bind specifically to Ψ in living cells.
source: We demonstrate that NC alone does not bind specifically to Ψ in living cells, whereas full-length Gag and a CANC subdomain bind to Ψ with high specificity.
evidence: Demonstrated through CLIP-seq experiments showing NC exhibits low-level indiscriminate binding across gRNA rather than specific Ψ binding.

claim: Full-length Gag binds to Ψ with high specificity in living cells.
source: We demonstrate that NC alone does not bind specifically to Ψ in living cells, whereas full-length Gag and a CANC subdomain bind to Ψ with high specificity.
evidence: Demonstrated through CLIP-seq experiments showing characteristic binding peaks at U5, SL1, and SL3/4 regions of Ψ.

claim: CANC subdomain binds to Ψ with high specificity in living cells.
source: We demonstrate that NC alone does not bind specifically to Ψ in living cells, whereas full-length Gag and a CANC subdomain bind to Ψ with high specificity.
evidence: Demonstrated through CLIP-seq experiments showing characteristic binding peaks at U5, SL1, and SL3/4 regions of Ψ.

claim: Perturbation of the Ψ RNA structure affects CANC:Ψ binding specificity.
source: Perturbation of the Ψ RNA structure or NC zinc fingers affected CANC:Ψ binding specificity.
evidence: CLIP experiments with Ψ mutants (DIS-GAGA and InsGGAA) showed altered binding patterns compared to wild-type.

claim: Perturbation of NC zinc fingers affects CANC:Ψ binding specificity.
source: Perturbation of the Ψ RNA structure or NC zinc fingers affected CANC:Ψ binding specificity.
evidence: CLIP experiments with zinc finger deletion mutants (dZF1, dZF2, dZF) showed marked reduction or abolishment of specific Ψ binding.

claim: CANC variants with substitutions that disrupt CA:CA dimer, trimer, or hexamer interfaces in the immature Gag lattice affect RNA binding.
source: Notably, CANC variants with substitutions that disrupt CA:CA dimer, trimer, or hexamer interfaces in the immature Gag lattice also affected RNA binding, and mutants that were unable to assemble a nascent Gag lattice were unable to specifically bind to Ψ.
evidence: Multiple CA substitution mutants targeting different interfaces showed impaired Ψ binding in CLIP experiments and reduced multimerization in BMH crosslinking experiments.

claim: Mutants that are unable to assemble a nascent Gag lattice are unable to specifically bind to Ψ.
source: Notably, CANC variants with substitutions that disrupt CA:CA dimer, trimer, or hexamer interfaces in the immature Gag lattice also affected RNA binding, and mutants that were unable to assemble a nascent Gag lattice were unable to specifically bind to Ψ.
evidence: CANC mutants with severe multimerization defects (e.g., A22D, A42D, W184A/M185A) failed to bind specifically to Ψ in CLIP experiments.

claim: Artificially multimerized NC domains do not specifically bind Ψ.
source: Artificially multimerized NC domains did not specifically bind Ψ.
evidence: Chimeric NC fusion proteins with GCN4pII, GCN4pAA, or ccHex2 multimerization domains exhibited low-level indiscriminate binding across gRNA in CLIP experiments.

claim: CA variants with substitutions in inositol phosphate coordinating residues that prevent CA hexamerization are deficient in Ψ binding.
source: CA variants with substitutions in inositol phosphate coordinating residues that prevent CA hexamerization were also deficient in Ψ binding and second-site revertant mutants that restored CA assembly also restored specific binding to Ψ.
evidence: CANC K158A and CANC K227A mutants exhibited deficits in Ψ binding in CLIP experiments.

claim: Second-site revertant mutants that restore CA assembly also restore specific binding to Ψ.
source: CA variants with substitutions in inositol phosphate coordinating residues that prevent CA hexamerization were also deficient in Ψ binding and second-site revertant mutants that restored CA assembly also restored specific binding to Ψ.
evidence: CANC K158A/SP1 T8I and CANC K227A/SP1 T8I double mutants restored specific Ψ binding in CLIP experiments.

claim: The correct assembly of a nascent immature CA lattice is required for the specific interaction between Gag and Ψ in cells.
source: Overall, these data indicate that the correct assembly of a nascent immature CA lattice is required for the specific interaction between Gag and Ψ in cells.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence from CLIP and crosslinking experiments with various CA mutants support this conclusion.

claim: HIV-1 gRNA is the dominant RNA species in virions despite being present among a vast excess of host RNAs in the cytosol.
source: HIV-1 gRNA is present among a vast excess of host RNAs in the cytosol of infected cells, yet it is the dominant RNA species in virions (Rulli et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rulli et al., 2007.

claim: The specific encapsidation of HIV-1 gRNA into virions is attributed to the specific interaction between HIV-1 Gag and the viral packaging signal 'Ψ'.
source: The specific encapsidation of HIV-1 gRNA into virions is attributed to the specific interaction between HIV-1 Gag and the viral packaging signal 'Ψ' (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Berkowitz et al., 1996; Clavel and Orenstein, 1990; Clever et al., 1995; Clever et al., 2000; Darlix et al., 1990; D'Souza and Summers, 2005; Lever et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to foundational studies.

claim: Point mutations or deletions disrupting the zinc fingers of NC interfere with the specific packaging of gRNA.
source: The NC domain binds directly to RNA, and point mutations or deletions disrupting the zinc fingers of NC interfere with the specific packaging of gRNA (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Gorelick et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by data in this study showing zinc finger deletions reduce Ψ binding.

claim: Full-length Gag or CANC has different RNA binding specificity compared to NC.
source: Indeed, RNase protection assays, yeast-three hybrid assays, and in vitro binding assays suggest that full-length Gag or CANC has different RNA binding specificity compared to NC, and some studies indicate binding to Ψ with higher specificity than NC (Bacharach and Goff, 1998; Damgaard et al., 1998; Guo et al., 2020; Kroupa et al., 2020; Webb et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Gag mutants with CA mutations exhibited reduced gRNA selectivity in an in vitro reconstituted HIV-1 Ψ packaging system.
source: Moreover, Gag mutants with CA mutations exhibited reduced gRNA selectivity in an in vitro reconstituted HIV-1 Ψ packaging system (Carlson et al., 2016), while Gag mutants with CA assembly deficits cannot initiate gRNA packaging (Duchon et al., 2021; Kutluay et al., 2014; Kutluay and Bieniasz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carlson et al., 2016.

claim: Gag mutants with CA assembly deficits cannot initiate gRNA packaging.
source: Moreover, Gag mutants with CA mutations exhibited reduced gRNA selectivity in an in vitro reconstituted HIV-1 Ψ packaging system (Carlson et al., 2016), while Gag mutants with CA assembly deficits cannot initiate gRNA packaging (Duchon et al., 2021; Kutluay et al., 2014; Kutluay and Bieniasz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duchon et al., 2021; Kutluay et al., 2014; Kutluay and Bieniasz, 2010.

claim: The RNA binding profile of the CANC protein to the HIV-1 genome is similar to that of the full-length Gag protein.
source: Crucially, the RNA binding profile of the CANC protein to the HIV-1 genome was similar to that of the full-length Gag protein, with a marginally higher fraction of reads mapping to Ψ.
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data comparing Gag and CANC binding profiles.

claim: CANC exhibits a marginally higher fraction of reads mapping to Ψ compared to full-length Gag.
source: Crucially, the RNA binding profile of the CANC protein to the HIV-1 genome was similar to that of the full-length Gag protein, with a marginally higher fraction of reads mapping to Ψ.
evidence: Observed in CLIP-seq data comparing Gag and CANC.

claim: The apparently enhanced preference of CANC for Ψ is because membrane-bound Gag, which exhibits more promiscuous binding to the viral genome, is not present when CANC is used.
source: We speculate that this apparently enhanced preference of CANC for Ψ is because the membrane bound Gag, that exhibits more promiscuous binding to the viral genome (Kutluay et al., 2014), is not present when CANC is used.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data, supported by citation to Kutluay et al., 2014.

claim: Both full-length Gag and CANC exhibit characteristic binding to Ψ involving three 'peaks' of read intensity corresponding to U5, SL1, and SL3/4.
source: Both the full-length Gag protein and CANC exhibited characteristic binding to Ψ involving three 'peaks' of read intensity corresponding to U5, SL1, and SL3/4 that are brought into proximity in the folded minimal packaging structure (Bieniasz and Telesnitsky, 2018; Lu et al., 2011; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B and C, consistent with known Ψ structure.

claim: The CANC InsGGAA Ψ mutant is bound comparatively poorly by CANC, with failure of the 3' portion of Ψ to bind CANC.
source: While CANC bound to the unmanipulated Ψ sequence with high specificity, the CANC InsGGAA Ψ mutant was bound comparatively poorly by CANC, with failure of the 3' portion of Ψ to bind CANC (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The exposure of the 5'-cap of gRNA to the translational machinery due to 'GGAA' insertion inhibits gRNA packaging.
source: This finding is consistent with previous studies showing that the exposure of the 5'-cap of gRNA to the translational machinery due to 'GGAA' insertion inhibits gRNA packaging (Ding et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2021 and consistent with observed CLIP data.

claim: The CANC DIS-GAGA Ψ mutant is bound by CANC specifically within the Ψ element, but with the exclusion of the SL1 stem-loop.
source: The CANC DIS-GAGA Ψ mutant, which presumably favors the retention of a monomeric RNA, was bound by CANC specifically within the Ψ element, but with the exclusion of the SL1 stem-loop (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Other Ψ elements are retained in the DIS-GAGA structure as in native dimer.
source: This finding is consistent with previous findings that other Ψ elements are retained in the DIS-GAGA structure as in native dimer (Keane et al., 2015) and suggests that the dimerized RNA elements are part of the structure recognized by Gag.
evidence: Supported by citation to Keane et al., 2015 and consistent with CLIP data.

claim: The dimerized RNA elements are part of the structure recognized by Gag.
source: This finding is consistent with previous findings that other Ψ elements are retained in the DIS-GAGA structure as in native dimer (Keane et al., 2015) and suggests that the dimerized RNA elements are part of the structure recognized by Gag.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DIS-GAGA mutant shows altered binding pattern, specifically loss of SL1 binding.

claim: The tertiary structure of the Ψ element is important for accurate recognition by Gag.
source: Overall, these results validate the utility of the CLIP method used herein and are consistent with the finding that the tertiary, and to some extent the quaternary, structure of the Ψ element is important for accurate recognition by Gag.
evidence: Inferred from CLIP data showing that Ψ structure perturbations affect CANC binding.

claim: The quaternary structure of the Ψ element is important for accurate recognition by Gag.
source: Overall, these results validate the utility of the CLIP method used herein and are consistent with the finding that the tertiary, and to some extent the quaternary, structure of the Ψ element is important for accurate recognition by Gag.
evidence: Inferred from CLIP data showing that dimerization-defective mutants affect CANC binding.

claim: The deletion of either zinc finger in the NC domain causes a marked reduction in specific Ψ binding.
source: The deletion of either zinc finger in the NC domain caused a marked reduction in specific Ψ binding, while the deletion of both zinc fingers nearly completely abolished specific Ψ binding, despite the presence of similar levels of protein for each of the mutant CANC proteins (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The deletion of both zinc fingers nearly completely abolishes specific Ψ binding.
source: The deletion of either zinc finger in the NC domain caused a marked reduction in specific Ψ binding, while the deletion of both zinc fingers nearly completely abolished specific Ψ binding, despite the presence of similar levels of protein for each of the mutant CANC proteins (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: NC is required for the specific interaction between Gag and Ψ.
source: This observation is consistent with earlier findings that NC is required for the specific interaction between Gag and Ψ (Aldovini and Young, 1990; Didierlaurent et al., 2011; Dorfman et al., 1993; Gorelick et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and confirmed by zinc finger deletion data in this study.

claim: NC alone is not sufficient to bind specifically to Ψ.
source: CLIP experiments using this construct revealed that NC was well expressed but was not sufficient to bind specifically to Ψ. Instead, low read counts, distributed across the entire HIV-1 genome, were obtained (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data showing NC exhibits non-specific binding across the genome.

claim: The deficit in specific Ψ binding associated with CA deletion is as profound as the deficit associated with deletion of both NC zinc fingers.
source: Indeed, the deficit in specific Ψ binding associated with CA deletion was as profound as the deficit associated with deletion of both NC zinc fingers (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing CLIP-seq data for NC construct and CANC dZF construct in Figure 2B.

claim: The chimeric proteins GCN4pII-SP1-NC, GCN4pAA-SP1-NC, and ccHex2-SP1-NC are able to form multimers, up to and including hexamers.
source: The chimeric proteins were expressed at level similar to CANC and were able to form multimers, up to and including hexamers, as indicated by the appearance of BMH crosslinked species (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by BMH crosslinking western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: The chimeric, multimeric NC fusion proteins do not bind specifically to Ψ.
source: Nevertheless, the chimeric, multimeric NC fusion proteins did not bind specifically to Ψ (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1); instead, they exhibited low-level indiscriminate binding across the gRNA, similar to the isolated monomeric NC domain (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CA is required for the specific interaction between CANC and Ψ.
source: These results suggest that CA is required for the specific interaction between CANC and Ψ and that CA provides some function beyond simple multimerization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that artificially multimerized NC does not bind Ψ specifically, while CANC does.

claim: CA provides some function beyond simple multimerization.
source: These results suggest that CA is required for the specific interaction between CANC and Ψ and that CA provides some function beyond simple multimerization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that artificially multimerized NC does not bind Ψ specifically, while CANC does.

claim: CANC mutants that readily form high-order multimers in the cytoplasm bind to Ψ with high specificity.
source: Comparison of the behaviors of the CANC mutants in CLIP experiments and in vivo cytoplasmic chemical crosslinking experiments revealed a correlation between CA multimerization and Ψ-specific binding: CANC mutants that were readily able to form high-order multimers in the cytoplasm bound to Ψ with high specificity, similar to the wild-type CANC (in the cases of R18A/N21A, P38A, E45A, Q219A, SP1 T8I, and SP1 T12A).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing BMH crosslinking data (Figure 4A) with CLIP data (Figure 4B-C) for multiple mutants.

claim: CANC mutants with deficits in cytoplasmic multimerization fail to bind specifically to Ψ.
source: Conversely, mutants that had deficits in cytoplasmic multimerization failed to bind specifically to Ψ.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing BMH crosslinking data (Figure 4A) with CLIP data (Figure 4B-C) for multiple mutants.

claim: Impairment of Ψ binding imposed by CA substitutions occurs irrespective of which interface (twofold, threefold, or sixfold) is targeted.
source: Notably, impairment of Ψ binding imposed by CA substitutions occurred irrespective of which interface (twofold, threefold, or sixfold) was targeted.
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP data showing that mutants targeting different interfaces all show Ψ binding defects.

claim: The ability of CANC to form a nascent immature lattice is important for specific recognition of Ψ.
source: Overall, these experiments suggest that the ability of CANC to form a nascent immature lattice is important for specific recognition of Ψ.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between multimerization ability and Ψ binding specificity across multiple CA mutants.

claim: CA mutants that generate extracellular virions in the context of full-length HIV-1 NL4-3 show only minor variations in vRNA:Gag ratios.
source: Nevertheless, these mutants were able to generate extracellular particles in the context of full-length HIV-1 NL4-3. There were only minor variations in the vRNA:Gag ratios for these mutants, suggesting that they are able to package vRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR quantification of vRNA and p24 levels shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: CA mutants that generate virions must have assembled an immature Gag lattice.
source: However, given that these mutants generated extracellular virions, they must, by definition, have been able to assemble. An essential step in assembly is the generation of an immature Gag lattice. Thus, these mutant full-length Gag proteins must have assembled an immature Gag lattice, despite the fact that the CANC proteins do not appear to assemble into higher-order multimers in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Logical inference based on the requirement for lattice assembly to produce virions.

claim: Membrane binding can suppress both the Gag multimerization and Ψ binding deficits exhibited by some CA mutants.
source: We posit that the CA mutants that generate virions in the context of full-length virus but do not generate high-order CANC multimers in the cytosol, harbor partial defects in immature lattice formation that are evident in the context of CANC in the cytosol but are at least partly suppressed when Gag is targeted to membrane in the context of a full-length Gag protein.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some mutants defective in cytosolic CANC multimerization can still produce virions with normal vRNA:Gag ratios.

claim: Immature lattice assembly can occur either in the cytosol or at the plasma membrane to enable Ψ recognition.
source: Notably, these results do not alter the interpretation that immature lattice assembly is required for Ψ binding but do suggest that immature lattice assembly can occur either in the cytosol or at the plasma membrane to enable Ψ recognition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that membrane-targeted full-length Gag can overcome some assembly defects seen with cytosolic CANC.

claim: IP6 is required for the assembly of the immature Gag lattice in cells.
source: The abundant intracellular small molecule inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) coordinates two rings of positively charged lysine residues formed by K158 and K227 at the base of the CA hexamer (Dick et al., 2018). As such, it is required for the assembly of the immature Gag lattice in cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dick et al., 2018 and established knowledge in the field.

claim: CANC K158A and CANC K227A mutants exhibit deficits in Ψ binding.
source: Both CANC K158A and CANC K227A mutants exhibited deficits in Ψ binding (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A lattice stabilizing substitution in SP1 (SP1 T8I) restores virion assembly and viral infectivity in K158A and K227A mutants.
source: A second-site revertant of K158A and K227A, specifically a lattice stabilizing substitution in SP1(SP1 T8I), restores virion assembly and viral infectivity (Mallery et al., 2021; Poston et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mallery et al., 2021 and Poston et al., 2021.

claim: Introduction of SP1 T8I substitution enables otherwise Ψ-binding defective CANC proteins (K158A and K227A) to bind Ψ with high specificity.
source: Notably, introduction of this second-site substitution (in CANC K158A/SP1 T8I and CANC K227A/SP1 T8I) enabled otherwise Ψ-binding defective CANC proteins to bind Ψ with high specificity (Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: The specific binding to Ψ requires the correct assembly of the nascent viral immature CA lattice.
source: Thus, these results reinforce the conclusion that the specific binding to Ψ requires the correct assembly of the nascent viral immature CA lattice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that second-site revertants that restore lattice assembly also restore Ψ binding.

claim: The initiation of the assembly of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice in infected cells is required for the maintenance of the interaction between Gag/CANC and the Ψ element of the gRNA.
source: We conclude that the initiation of the assembly of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice in infected cells is required for the maintenance of the interaction between Gag/CANC and the Ψ element of the gRNA.
evidence: Overall conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence from CLIP and crosslinking experiments.

claim: A small number of Gag molecules (below the limit of detection by fluorescent microscopy) is involved in initial Gag/gRNA complex formation.
source: Imaging studies of the HIV-1 virion assembly process suggest that a small number of Gag molecules (below the limit of detection by fluorescent microscopy) is involved in initial Gag/gRNA complex formation (Hendrix et al., 2015; Jouvenet et al., 2009; Kutluay and Bieniasz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: The ability of CANC to multimerize into higher-order multimers (such as 10-mers or greater) in in vivo chemical crosslinking experiments predicts specific Ψ binding.
source: However, the ability of CANC to multimerize into higher-order multimers (such as 10-mers or greater) in our in vivo chemical crosslinking experiments predicted specific Ψ binding, and the twofold, threefold, and sixfold CA interaction interfaces are all required.
evidence: Observed correlation between BMH crosslinking patterns and CLIP results across multiple mutants.

claim: The twofold, threefold, and sixfold CA interaction interfaces are all required for specific Ψ binding.
source: However, the ability of CANC to multimerize into higher-order multimers (such as 10-mers or greater) in our in vivo chemical crosslinking experiments predicted specific Ψ binding, and the twofold, threefold, and sixfold CA interaction interfaces are all required.
evidence: Demonstrated by the fact that mutants targeting any of these interfaces show Ψ binding defects.

claim: High-order multimers of CANC may be needed to recognize Ψ.
source: These findings suggest that perhaps high-order multimers of CANC may be needed to recognize Ψ.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on crosslinking and CLIP data.

claim: CA may be required to precisely position NC domains within a hexamer to permit specific Ψ binding.
source: Alternatively, it is also possible that CA is required to precisely position NC domains within a hexamer to permit specific Ψ binding.
evidence: Alternative speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: There are at least 10 potential Gag/NC interaction sites in gRNA which are important for packaging.
source: Several lines of evidence from previously published work are consistent with the proposition that high-order Gag multimers bind to Ψ: (1) SHAPE and XL-SHAPE experiments identified at least 10 potential Gag/NC interaction sites in gRNA which are important for packaging (Kenyon et al., 2015; Wilkinson et al., 2008);
evidence: Supported by citations to Kenyon et al., 2015 and Wilkinson et al., 2008.

claim: At least 20 Gag molecules are needed to form a complete Gag/leader gRNA dimer complex.
source: (2) electrophoretic mobility shift experiments suggest that at least 20 Gag molecules were needed to form a complete Gag/leader gRNA dimer complex (D'Souza et al., 2021);
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Souza et al., 2021.

claim: There are at least two dozen high-affinity NC-binding sites in a dimerization competent form gRNA.
source: (3) studies of NC and Ψ interactions with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) suggest that there are at least two dozen high-affinity NC-binding sites in a dimerization competent form gRNA (Ding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2020.

claim: The W184A/M185A mutant is mainly monomeric under crosslinking conditions despite W184/M185 being located at an inter-hexamer interface.
source: There were some unexpected findings from our chemical crosslinking experiments. For example, the W184A/M185A mutant was mainly monomeric under the crosslinking conditions in our assay, despite the fact that W184/M185 are located at an inter-hexamer interface rather than an intra-hexamer interface.
evidence: Observed in BMH crosslinking data in Figure 4A.

claim: A CA quadruple mutant A14C/E45C/W184A/M185A was able to form a hexamer under reducing conditions.
source: In a previous report, a CA quadruple mutant A14C/E45C/W184A/M185A was able to form a hexamer under reducing conditions (Pornillos et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pornillos et al., 2009.

claim: Both dimer and trimer CA interfaces contribute to the formation of early lattice assembly intermediates.
source: This result, along with the fact that the dimer interface mutants E28A/E29A and W184A/M185A mutants were also mainly monomeric in cells, suggests that both dimer and trimer CA interfaces contribute to the formation of early lattice assembly intermediates.
evidence: Inferred from BMH crosslinking data showing multiple interface mutants fail to form dimers.

claim: Inter-hexamer contacts are important for hexamer assembly.
source: Moreover, mutants that failed to form crosslinkable dimers via inter-hexamer contacts also failed to form hexamers, suggesting that inter-hexamer contacts are important for hexamer assembly.
evidence: Inferred from BMH crosslinking data showing dimer interface mutants also fail to form hexamers.

claim: Previous models which proposed that trimer-of-dimers of CA are basic building block of the HIV-1 immature lattice are not consistent with the crosslinking results.
source: Thus, previous models (Grime and Voth, 2012; Tomasini et al., 2018; Tsiang et al., 2012) which proposed that trimer-of-dimers of CA are basic building block of the HIV-1 immature lattice are not consistent with our crosslinking results.
evidence: Inferred from crosslinking data showing that disruption of any interface prevents higher-order assembly.

claim: All three CA-CA interaction interfaces (twofold, threefold, and sixfold) contribute simultaneously to immature lattice formation.
source: Overall, the results of the crosslinking experiments suggest that all the three CA-CA interaction interfaces (twofold, threefold, and sixfold interaction interfaces) contribute simultaneously to immature lattice formation since disruptions of either twofold (W184A/M185A), threefold (A22D and A42D), or sixfold (D197A, G222A, P224A, and SP1 M4A) CA-CA interaction interfaces lead to overall defects rather than the formation of discrete low-order multimeric species.
evidence: Inferred from BMH crosslinking data showing that disruption of any interface leads to overall assembly defects.

claim: Membrane anchoring can increase the efficiency of RNA packaging.
source: Recently, Duchon et al. used complementation approaches with Gag proteins whose multimerization was driven by leucine-zippers to show that membrane anchoring can increase the efficiency of RNA packaging, whether driven by interactions between NC and Ψ or by an artificial RNA binding protein:RNA target pair (Duchon et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duchon et al., 2021.

claim: Membrane binding is not required for CANC-Ψ interaction in the cytoplasm of cells.
source: Nevertheless, our study shows that membrane binding is not required for CANC-Ψ interaction in the cytoplasm of cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by CLIP experiments showing CANC (which lacks membrane-targeting MA domain) binds Ψ specifically.

claim: The actual site of Gag-Ψ interaction could change as Gag accumulates in infected cells.
source: Given that the localization of Gag can change with its concentration in cells, it is possible that the actual site of Gag-Ψ interaction could also change as Gag accumulates in infected cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known Gag localization dynamics.

claim: Membrane binding can suppress both the Gag multimerization and Ψ binding deficits exhibited by some CA mutants.
source: This finding suggests that membrane binding can suppress both the Gag multimerization and Ψ binding deficits exhibited by some CA mutants and, thus, that Ψ binding can, in principle, occur at the plasma membrane or in the cytosol, provided that higher order multimerization occurs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some mutants defective in cytosolic CANC assembly can still package RNA when expressed as full-length Gag.

claim: Ψ binding can occur at the plasma membrane or in the cytosol, provided that higher order multimerization occurs.
source: This finding suggests that membrane binding can suppress both the Gag multimerization and Ψ binding deficits exhibited by some CA mutants and, thus, that Ψ binding can, in principle, occur at the plasma membrane or in the cytosol, provided that higher order multimerization occurs.
evidence: Inferred from data showing both cytosolic CANC and membrane-bound Gag can bind Ψ.

claim: CA is essential for the specific interaction between HIV-1 Gag and Ψ.
source: Overall, our study shows that CA is essential for the specific interaction between HIV-1 Gag and Ψ.
evidence: Overall conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: CA is key for controlling the morphology of HIV-1 particle assembly.
source: CA is therefore key, not only for controlling the morphology of HIV-1 particle assembly but also for selective viral genome packaging.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field.

claim: CA is key for selective viral genome packaging.
source: CA is therefore key, not only for controlling the morphology of HIV-1 particle assembly but also for selective viral genome packaging.
evidence: Demonstrated by data in this study showing CA is required for specific Ψ binding.

claim: HIV-1, HIV-2, and SIV Gag can co-assemble and package each other's genome.
source: Based on the evidence that HIV-1, HIV-2, and SIV Gag can co-assemble and package each other's genome (Al Shamsi et al., 2011; Franke et al., 1994; Motomura et al., 2008; Rizvi and Panganiban, 1993) and the conservation of primary and tertiary Gag structures between these viruses, the insights gained from this study are likely applicable across primate lentiviruses.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing cross-packaging.

claim: The insights gained from this study are likely applicable across primate lentiviruses.
source: Based on the evidence that HIV-1, HIV-2, and SIV Gag can co-assemble and package each other's genome (Al Shamsi et al., 2011; Franke et al., 1994; Motomura et al., 2008; Rizvi and Panganiban, 1993) and the conservation of primary and tertiary Gag structures between these viruses, the insights gained from this study are likely applicable across primate lentiviruses.
evidence: Inferred from conservation of Gag structures and cross-packaging ability.

claim: The CLIP procedure uses an infrared-dye-conjugated 3' adaptor in place of a conventional radioactive labeled 3' adaptor.
source: In this CLIP procedure, an infrared-dye-conjugated 3' adaptor (Zarnegar et al., 2016) is used in place of a conventional radioactive labeled 3' adaptor.
evidence: Methodological description of the CLIP procedure used in this study.

claim: Protein-RNA crosslinking is driven by metabolic 4-thiouridine incorporation into target RNA.
source: Protein-RNA crosslinking is driven by metabolic 4-thiouridine incorporation into target RNA (Hafner et al., 2010), and the labeled adaptor is ligated to protein/RNA crosslinked species directly on antibody-conjugated Dynabeads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Methodological description supported by citation to Hafner et al., 2010.

claim: The labeled adaptor is ligated to protein/RNA crosslinked species directly on antibody-conjugated Dynabeads.
source: Protein-RNA crosslinking is driven by metabolic 4-thiouridine incorporation into target RNA (Hafner et al., 2010), and the labeled adaptor is ligated to protein/RNA crosslinked species directly on antibody-conjugated Dynabeads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Methodological description of the modified CLIP procedure.

claim: The methodological adjustments cut the experimental time by half without loss of sensitivity.
source: These methodological adjustments cut the experimental time by half without loss of sensitivity, enabling higher throughput in CLIP assays.
evidence: Claimed benefit of the modified CLIP method.

claim: MA is not involved in the initial Gag:gRNA interaction in the cytosol.
source: As we intended to study the initial Gag:gRNA interaction in the cytosol and MA is not involved in this process (Bou-Nader et al., 2021; Kutluay et al., 2014), we also generated a proviral construct (referred to as pCANC) in which the start codon of MA (ATG) was mutated to abolish MA expression;
evidence: Supported by citations to Bou-Nader et al., 2021 and Kutluay et al., 2014.
